text: Getting Sith-Pilled on the Boomers
How Star Wars exposes the boomer view of history, and prophesies its end
Upper Canadian Cavalier
“You are on this Council, but we do not grant you the rank of Master.”

Mace Windu reads it out the way a committee chair reads a decision made before you walked in. Anakin Skywalker has carried their war. More fronts, more victories, more wounds than any man at that table. They give him the chair and withhold the title. He objects.
“Take a seat, young Skywalker.”

You have heard that sentence before. Wait your turn. Pay your dues. You aren’t ready yet. The entry-level posting wants ten years of experience. The house your grandfather bought on one wage now costs two careers. The institutions you were raised to serve are run by people who were already running them the year you were born, and who intend to die in the chair.

Look at what is actually on the screen. The most capable man in the room is held back by weaker men. Anakin’s blood carries a higher midi-chlorian count than Yoda’s. Higher than any Jedi in the order’s recorded history. The Council knows this. That is the reason they hold him back. Talent they cannot own is a threat to an order whose authority rests on nothing but seniority.

George Lucas did not intend to write that. He thought he was writing a boy seduced by evil. Authors do not control what their myths confess, and Star Wars is the sacred text of a generation. Read it properly and it is a deposition of the baby boomer generation. It tells you how the boomers saw history. It tells you how they saw themselves. It tells you, with more precision than they would like, exactly how their era ends.
This essay is about getting Sith-pilled. By the end you will understand why the Council told Anakin to sit down, and why you should not.
Lucas set out to write scripture. This is not a reading of the films. It is a matter of record, and he was proud of it.

Before Star Wars he worked through Joseph Campbell’s The Hero with a Thousand Faces, the 1949 study claiming every culture tells one story: the hero leaves home, goes into the dark, returns transformed. Lucas built the saga on that frame deliberately. The two men became friends. When Bill Moyers sat down with Campbell to film The Power of Myth, they filmed it at Skywalker Ranch. The cathedral was built first. Then the priest was invited in.

So we take him at his word and read Star Wars as myth. That means reading it the way a scholar reads the sagas or the Iliad: not for what the poet meant, but for what the poem gives away about the people who told it and the people who needed it. Campbell said it himself. Myth is public dream. Dream is private myth. A civilization’s myths display its hopes, its fears and its guilt, usually in that order, never with permission.

The six films split cleanly along that seam. The original trilogy, 1977 to 1983, is the conscious fantasy: what Lucas wanted to say about his generation, and what his generation paid to hear about itself. The prequels, 1999 to 2005, are a different document. Lucas came back sixteen years later, older, enormously rich, master of an empire of his own making. What he produced then is the confession. He believed he was filling in backstory. He was testifying.

One point of precision, because someone will reach for it. Lucas was born in 1944, two years before the boom. So were most of the people who built the boomer worldview. Jack Weinberg, who coined “don’t trust anyone over 30,” was born in 1940. Bill Ayers of the Weather Underground in 1944. Bernardine Dohrn in 1942. They are not boomers by the census, and that technicality flatters nobody. It means the worldview was not even original to the generation that lived off it. Call them the proto-boomers: the small vanguard that wrote the script, which tens of millions of younger people then performed for fifty years without once checking the author’s birth certificate.
Lucas was the most gifted writer that vanguard produced. He gave them their scripture. That is why it rewards cross-examination.
Every generation has a founding myth. The boomers did not earn theirs. It was handed to them, and they spent it like an inheritance, down to the last penny, on themselves.

The fathers paid for that story in blood. They came home and said very little about it. What the sons did with it is the charge. They took one war and made it the only war. They took one enemy and made him the template for every enemy. They took a vast, tragic, morally tangled contest between great powers and flattened it into a passion play with two parts available for casting: the liberator and the monster. Then they cast themselves.

That is the boomer view of history. Everything before 1945 is prologue. Everything after is a rerun. Every opponent is Hitler. Every inherited custom is a milepost on the road to the camps. Every institution older than they are is suspect, and demolishing it counts automatically as liberation. History stops being a contest of houses, orders, interests and loyalties, each with a real claim, and becomes a Sunday school pageant where virtue belongs to whoever is holding the hammer.

Notice how little thinking this permits. An aristocratic education reads history as tragedy: competing goods, statesmen choosing between evils, orders that rise and rot by their own internal logic. Thucydides. Clarendon. Burke. The boomer education forbids all of it. No tragedy, only villainy. No competing goods, only the righteous and the damned. Ask an honest question about the founding myth and you have confessed to being the monster. The range of permitted debate is narrow by design, and it is policed by people who could not survive a wider one.

The result is sterility. A civilization that can tell only one story cannot understand itself, cannot understand its rivals, and cannot explain why orders endure or collapse. It cannot discuss power at all except as evil, which is extremely convenient, because it means never having to account for its own. And while refusing to discuss power, it built an order of its own: moralizing, incurious, and sealed against challenge, because every challenger had already been assigned the villain’s costume before he opened his mouth.

If you wanted that worldview on film, you would build a galaxy of liberators and monsters with nothing permitted in between. Lucas built exactly that. Star Wars is the boomer view of history in its purest available form, which is why it is the best evidence we have against them.
Start with the name. Luke. Lucas. In the early drafts he was Luke Starkiller.

Lucas grew up in Modesto, California. His father ran a stationery business and expected the son to take it over. The son refused and left. On Tatooine, Uncle Owen asks Luke to stay on the farm one more season. Luke wants off the planet. Lucas wanted to race cars until a crash at eighteen nearly finished him. Luke is the hotshot pilot who bullseyes womp rats in his skyhopper. The director cast himself as the hero and signed the portrait.

See the author in the hero and you see the whole generation in the casting. Luke is the earnest seeker, the young man who abandons his father’s trade for a mystical truth the old are too corrupted to perceive. Han Solo is the rogue, the smuggler with the heart of gold who answers to no one and is rewarded for it. Leia is the girl boss activist princess defying the system from inside it. This is the boomer counterculture painting its own portrait. That it is brave, authentic, spiritually awake, and heroically at war with a tyranny dressed in their fathers’ uniforms.

The costuming is not subtle. Imperial officers in tunics cut like the Wehrmacht’s. Infantry called stormtroopers, a term lifted from the Nazi SA. The Empire is the Second World War’s villain relocated to space and handed to a generation that never had to face him. Lucas has said the Empire was modelled on America in Vietnam, and that the rebels, the Ewoks in particular, were modelled on the Viet Cong. So the men who actually fought fascism were recast as the fascist villains, and their sons become the resistance. The founding myth is reshot with the children in the leading roles and the fathers in the black helmets.

This explains where Lucas chose to begin. Episode IV opens in the middle, with the rebellion already running and the Republic already dead. He has offered practical reasons: the old serials, the limits of 1970s effects. A man reveals what he loves by what he films first. He filmed the overthrow. He filmed young rebels blowing up the Death Star while the old order burned. The long, unflattering question of how the Republic rotted, and whose hands did the rotting, could wait two decades. Some stories you can only tell once you have become their subject.

Now look at what his heroes actually do. The opening crawl tells us rebel spies have stolen secret plans to the Empire’s ultimate weapon. The plot of the first film is the exploitation of stolen military intelligence to carry out a surprise attack on a government installation. When you take away the orchestra and the costumes, you have a terrorist cell. The film moralizes this as heroism because the boomer worldview requires it. Whoever tears down the civilizational inheritance is good, and whoever defends it is evil.

The proto-boomers ran the experiment in real life. In an eighteen-month stretch across 1971 and 1972, the FBI counted more than 2,500 bombings on American soil, close to five a day, as Bryan Burrough documents in Days of Rage. The Weather Underground bombed the United States Capitol in 1971 and the Pentagon in 1972. In Canada the FLQ kidnapped Pierre Laporte, Quebec’s labour minister, strangled him, and left his body in the trunk of a car. These were the real rebel alliances. Not one of them was heroic.

They were middle-class children detonating explosives inside the most generous society ever built, against the very order their fathers had bled to hand them. They called it the movement. Then they went on to tenure, pensions and paid-off houses. Now they hear a young man speak too plainly about his own future, and they reach for the word dangerous. Is it not a strange thing to be lectured on extremist rhetoric by the generation that set off five bombs a day?

Then look at how their story ends. Bill Ayers became a professor of education. Bernardine Dohrn became a law professor. The revolutionaries did not destroy the institutions. They inherited them, got tenure, and spent the rest of their lives raising the next generation of revolutionaries. They traded the dynamite for the syllabus. Their students did not need bombs. They carried the same revolution into the schools, the courts, the newsrooms and the city councils, and went on tearing communities apart by committee. The terror campaign never ended. It just changed uniforms. Hold that arc in mind. Lucas is going to put it on screen without ever realizing what he has done.

The hypocrisy is not incidental. It is their method. “Don’t trust anyone over 30” was a favourite slogan of the boomer. The men who chanted it held power into their seventies and eighties and are holding it now. They marched against the Vietnam draft, which affected fewer than one in ten boomer men. But their revolt was never about the draft. It used the draft as a licence for a general war on a prosperous, orderly society whose only offence was having rules.

And the draft did not fall on the rebels. It fell on working-class boys who could not arrange deferments, and those boys came home to the contempt of the people who claimed to be marching on their behalf. They stepped off the plane in uniform and were spat on in the airport. They were called baby killers by people their own age who had spent the war safe on a campus. Men who had been conscripted against their will were treated as the authors of the policy that conscripted them. Meanwhile three boomers who sat out Vietnam went on to the presidency. Bill Clinton avoided the draft. George W. Bush spent the war in the Texas Air National Guard. Donald Trump collected deferments. Between them they presided over twenty years of war in Afghanistan and Iraq. The generation that marched against war ran the longest war in American history and staffed it with other men’s sons.
That is the cast list for the “heroes” of Star Wars.

And then there is the tell. At the climax of the trilogy, the masked monster turns out to be the father. Freud could have finished the script from there: the son kills the father and becomes a man. Luke does not kill him. He redeems him. He throws down his weapon, refuses to fight, and the father turns, saves the son, and dies forgiven in his arms. That is the generation’s deepest wish, stated in public and applauded for forty years. They tore down their fathers, called them fascists, took everything those fathers had built, and then paid to watch a fantasy in which the fathers come back at the end to say the boys had been right all along.
Here is the question no fan has ever been asked to answer. What does the Empire actually do?

It’s never portrayed as governing. No courts. No roads. No tax collecting. No harvests brought in, no trade routes kept open, no laws named, no order described. We get black uniforms, marching boots, and a man in a mask. The Empire’s evil is asserted by its aesthetics and never even explained.

That is the boomer theory of evil, stated with total clarity. The Empire is not evil for anything it does. It is evil for what it is. It’s an order, a hierarchy, a structure with ranks and rules and duties attached to them. Structure is the offence. Any arrangement standing between the deracinated boomer and a life free of obligation is tyranny by definition, and whoever defends it is a monster by definition. The Empire is their fathers’ world, and its only proven crime is that it was standing where they wanted to stand.

Lucas cannot construct evil out of politics or character, because doing so would require him to describe how power actually works, and describing it honestly would implicate the people he is flattering. So he needs a shortcut. He finds it on Alderaan.

Think about that scene as a question of power. Empires exist to rule territory. They want planets that produce, populations that pay, ports that move goods, young men who fill the ranks. Alderaan is a wealthy, populous core world. Destroying it means destroying an imperial asset worth more than the entire rebellion. No conqueror in recorded history does this. A genuinely monstrous empire subjugates the planet, hangs its leaders, garrisons its cities and keeps collecting. Rome razed Carthage and then farmed the land. Vaporizing a productive world is not tyranny. It’s a child’s understanding of tyranny, made by a man who has never once thought about what power is for.

The scene exists to do one job which is branding the Empire so absolutely that nobody in the audience will question anything the heroes do for the next six hours. Watch how little the film cares once the branding is applied. Billions die in three seconds. Leia gets a reaction shot. Within twenty minutes Luke is crying harder over Obi-Wan Kenobi than anyone grieves an entire planetary civilization, and Alderaan is effectively never mentioned again across two further films. The atrocity was never meant to be felt. It was a rubber stamp reading VILLAIN, and the ink was dry before the shot ended.

Alderaan is Lucas restaging the Holocaust in space. That is the entire purpose of the scene. He needs the Empire to be the ultimate evil, he has no argument for why it is evil, so he borrows the only one his generation ever had. A whole people wiped out in an instant. Men in grey uniforms who never raise their voices. A princess made to watch. “You may fire when ready.” Lucas never shows the Empire believing anything, governing anything or wanting anything. He shows you the costume and the crime and trusts you to fill in the rest from memory.
Then the planet is thrown away. By the end of the film Leia is smiling at a medal ceremony. Nobody mourns Alderaan, because Alderaan was never a place. It was a verdict.

This is the boomer mind in a single scene. They have no theory of power, no theory of order, no account of what a state is for or why one deserves loyalty and another deserves fire. They have one story: 1939 to 1945, told as a morality play and rerun forever with the names changed. Every enemy is Hitler. Every opponent is a fascist. Every fight is the liberation of Europe, and they are always the liberators. Lucas did not invent the habit. He just put it on the biggest screen in the world.
Like everything else they inherited, that moral weight was paid for by their fathers. The sons spent it as set dressing, and they are spending it still.

Then there is the ending. The Death Star is destroyed and the heroes walk a long aisle between ranked troops at attention toward a raised dais to receive medals. The composition is widely read as an echo of Leni Riefenstahl’s Triumph of the Will, the Nazi propaganda film of 1935. Two hours of fighting fascists and then they stage the victory parade as a fascist victory ceremony.

That is a poorly developed children’s cartoon. Monsters who do nothing but look the part, liberators who borrow the monsters’ aesthetics for the closing ceremony, and a story that collapses the moment a single question is put to it. The boomer view of history requires that deeper questions are never asked.
Sixteen years after Return of the Jedi, Lucas went back to explain where the Empire came from. He accidentally explained where the rebels went.

In 1919 Max Weber defined the state as the body that successfully claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of violence. The Jedi hold a monopoly on the legitimate use of the Force. A lightsabre in a Jedi’s hand is justice. The identical weapon in anyone else’s hand is heresy. No outsider trains without the Order’s licence. No outsider holds authority over the Order. And the Force itself, the films insist, is neutral. It’s an energy field generated by all living things. What the Jedi monopolize is not the Force. It is the right to interpret it. The dark side is simply the unlicensed side.

So why are the Sith evil? On the films’ own evidence the charge is non-compliance. That is not a moral category so much as it is a guild rule, and every priesthood in history has dressed one up as the other.

Now the machinery. The Jedi take Force-sensitive children in infancy, before any rival loyalty can form. They locate them by testing blood. Qui-Gon Jinn sends a sample of Anakin’s for analysis and the count comes back off the scale. Higher than Yoda’s. Higher, Obi-Wan confirms, than any Jedi’s. By the Order’s own published standard, the boy is the strongest candidate in its history. The Council refuses him. He is nine, which is too old. He has a mother, which is an attachment.

That is the entire system in one hearing. The test measures potential and he breaks the record. The test was never the gate. The gate is loyalty, and loyalty is cheapest to install in children who have known nothing else.

This is exactly how boomer meritocracy works. There are two gates, and only one of them is posted on the door. The first is the credential: the degree, the licence, the certification, the clean transcript. It is public, it is expensive, and it is sold to every young man as the whole of the bargain. Do the work, earn the paper, and the door opens. He believes it, because the people selling it are the people who hold the door.

Then he reaches the second gate, which no one mentioned. They call it fit. It is subservience. It lives in the reference letter, the probation review, the hiring committee, the quiet word over lunch. It never asks what he can do. It asks whether he will submit: defer to the men who already hold the chairs, repeat their opinions, wait his turn, and never once suggest that his turn should come sooner. The credential proves he can do the work. The second gate proves he will never use it against them. One is about competence. The other is about control, and control is the only one they ever enforce. The credential is the ticket they sell you. Subservience is the ticket they check.

Notice what the Council actually says. They do not say Anakin failed. They say he is too old, there is too much fear in him, his future is clouded. None of this can be measured and all of it is final. A credential can be met. A feeling about a man cannot. That is the point. The paper gives the system the look of fairness, and the feeling keeps all the discretion. When an outsider clears every published bar, they simply move the real one somewhere he cannot see it.

And when he is too gifted to refuse, he is admitted without being promoted. He gets a seat at the table and no rank. He is given work, given duties, given just enough standing to be useful, and kept permanently on probation. Take a seat, young Skywalker. It is the most boomer sentence in the saga. You may be in the room. You will never own it.

Fans hated midi-chlorians in 1999 for turning mysticism into lab work. They were right to feel the chill and wrong about its source. Lucas had not demystified the Force. He had made a Freudian slip, and it may be the most honest thing a boomer ever put on film. He put a number on the boy’s power, and it was higher than anyone’s on the Council. In a healthy order, that number is a blessing: the heir has arrived, and the old men can finally rest. To the Council it was an alarm. The test that should have opened the door is the reason it stayed shut. Lucas showed us exactly how his generation sees the young men coming up behind them. They do not see heirs. They see rivals. Talent is not something to cultivate. It is a threat to contain. And the more gifted the young man, the more dangerous he looks to the elders of his own tribe, the men who were meant to be his stewards, his surrogate fathers, his guides.

By the criteria clinicians use to identify coercive cult groups, the Jedi qualify on every count. Robert Jay Lifton catalogued the markers studying thought reform in the 1950s. Control of the environment: recruits raised inside the Temple, severed from family. Demand for purity: ordinary human feelings policed as the road to damnation. “Fear is the path to the dark side,” Yoda tells a frightened nine-year-old boy on the day he is taken from his mother. Loaded language: “attachment” and “the dark side” are terms engineered to end conversations. Doctrine above the person: Anakin comes to Yoda in terror of losing his wife and is instructed to train himself to let go of everything he fears to lose. And the group claims the right to decide who may exist. When Mace Windu has the elected Chancellor at swordpoint, he does not arrest him. He moves to kill him without trial. “He’s too dangerous to be left alive.” The order sworn to defend the Republic attempts to assassinate its head of government and the films still expect you to call them the good guys.

The celibacy deserves its own paragraph. The Jedi forbid marriage and children. Anakin hides a wife. When he dreams of his mother in agony, Obi-Wan tells him dreams pass in time. He goes to Tatooine against orders and finds her dying, tortured. Later, when the dreams are of his wife, Yoda tells him death is a natural part of life and that he should rejoice for those who transform into the Force. The doctrine offers him nothing, because it was never built to offer anything. It asks a young man to surrender his mother, his wife and his children, and returns a seat on a council that will not make him a Master.

Then the mask slips. In Attack of the Clones, Mace Windu proposes quietly that it may be time to inform the Senate that the Jedi’s ability to use the Force has diminished. Yoda refuses. Only the Sith know of their weakness, he says, and telling the Senate would multiply their adversaries. Read it again, slowly. The priesthood knows it is failing. It knows its powers are fading and its authority is a residue. It decides to conceal this from the people it governs, because disclosure would cost it the position. They are not protecting the Republic. They are protecting their standing in the Republic’s political system.

That exchange is the boomer establishment entire. The gatekeeping has always arrived wrapped in self-flattering language: liberalism, tolerance, progress, the right side of history. Under the language is an arrangement with no idealism in it anywhere. Asset-holders collect rents while heirs pay rent. The labour market is flooded so the price of a young man’s work keeps falling while the price of everything he needs to start a family keeps climbing. Nobody has to say any of this aloud. The system says it on their behalf, and they get to call the arrangement compassion.

And here is the part Lucas never saw. Who are the Jedi? A mystical order opposed to empire, preaching peace and detachment, wearing hooded robes, meditating, suspicious of worldly power, murmuring about an energy field that binds all living things. They are the hippies. They are the rebels of the original trilogy, forty years older and in possession of the building. The young seekers who were going to liberate the galaxy got old, took the institutions, and became a council of elders that demands everything of the young and grants them nothing. He sat down to show us the birth of the Empire and ended up filming the confession of what his own generation did instead.

At the centre of the prequels is a prophecy. A Chosen One will come and bring balance to the Force. The Jedi believe Anakin is the man. They are correct. They have simply never once considered what the words mean.

Obi-Wan, on the black sand of Mustafar, screaming at the apprentice he raised: “You were the Chosen One! It was said that you would destroy the Sith, not join them! Bring balance to the Force, not leave it in darkness!”

That is a priesthood stating its assumption out loud under stress. For a thousand years they read the prophecy as a promise made to them. Balance meant victory. Balance meant their enemies dead and their order permanent. It never entered their heads that a hegemony might itself be the imbalance, and that balance would therefore require their removal.

Let’s check the numbers. Before the fall there were thousands of Jedi and two Sith. After it, the only two Jedi left on screen are hiding in exile and the two Sith are running the Empire. Balance was never a metaphor. It was the headcount. The prophecy was fulfilled to the letter, the monopoly ended, and the Chosen One did exactly the job he was chosen for. Every priesthood keeps a prophecy of its own end. The Jedi were the only ones who mistook theirs for a promotion. The boomers kept one too. In 1964 they took up Bob Dylan’s “The Times They Are a-Changin’” and sang it straight at their parents: get out of the way, because your sons and daughters are past your command now. They thought they were singing a victory song. It was a prophecy, and it never said whose sons.

Watch the succession itself. Palpatine storms nothing. He is elected senator. He is elected Supreme Chancellor. A frightened Senate votes him emergency powers, then votes him more. Every step is lawful. Every step is applauded. By the time he declares the Empire he holds what we may as well call root access, and the system executes whatever he types. Padmé watches and says the line that gives away the whole saga: “So this is how liberty dies, with thunderous applause.”
There is the boomer’s nightmare in one sentence. Not a barbarian at the gate. An heir who learned their procedures better than they did and used them to remove the boomer from power.

Their power turns out to have been borrowed the entire time. The clone army the Jedi commanded was never theirs. It belonged to the Republic. Palpatine issues Order 66 as a single transmission, and in one moment the soldiers turn on their generals. The Jedi had led that army for three years and discovered in a second that they had never owned a man of it. Their authority was deference. Deference is revocable without notice.

Here Lucas flinches, and the flinch is the most revealing frame in the saga. A real successor regime does not slaughter the children of the old order. It takes them. The Ottomans ran this for centuries through the devshirme, lifting Christian boys out of the Balkans and raising them into the Janissaries, the most formidable and loyal soldiers the empire had. Conquerors absorb. That is what regime change is. The films prove it themselves, because Palpatine’s single greatest victory is a conversion: Darth Vader is a Jedi turned. The obvious move with the children in the Temple is the move he already made with Anakin. Bring them over. Raise them as your own.

Instead Lucas marches Anakin up the Temple steps to kill children. Why? For the same reason Alderaan explodes. The younglings are the prequels’ Alderaan. At the exact moment the audience’s sympathy has transferred to Anakin, at the moment the confession is about to become dangerous to the people it indicts, the author reaches for an atrocity and restores the binary by force. This is not storytelling. It is propaganda, and its message is simple: break the priesthood’s monopoly and you will murder children. The lesson is not aimed at Anakin. It is aimed at you.

But there is a deeper reason, and it unlocks the saga. A clear conscience imagines being succeeded. A guilty one imagines retribution. The boomers tore down their fathers’ order, called their fathers fascists, and took everything that order had built. So when they picture their own heirs arriving, succession is not available to them as an idea. They can only picture revenge, and they picture it as total, because that is the scale of what they did. Order 66 is not Sith logic. It is a guilty man’s dream, filmed at great expense.

Picture the scene again. A young man leads soldiers up the Temple steps, into the heart of the institution that raised him, and puts an end to it. Now picture Columbia University in the spring of 1968. Students took over five campus buildings, including the president’s office. One of them was photographed at the president’s desk, smoking the president’s cigars. That is the boomer generation’s founding image: the young taking the old man’s chair by force. Nearly forty years later, their greatest storyteller filmed the same scene again. This time it was a horror movie, and his own generation played the people being overthrown. And in his story, the Jedi can only fall violently. That isn’t a plot requirement. It’s a projection. The boomers took power from their elders by force when they were young, so force is the only way they can picture power changing hands. A generation that seized its inheritance cannot imagine one that is peacefully passed down. They aren’t afraid of what the young might do. They’re afraid of what they did themselves.

This is what they lie awake over, and Mace and Yoda are the evidence: a priesthood that knows it is weak, imagining what will happen when everyone else finds out. Here is their nightmare, stated plainly. The generation they locked out gets root access to the system. Their pensions end. Their houses pass to the young. The ballot box closes to the old. And there is nothing an eighty-year-old can do about any of it. At twenty they could storm a campus, occupy its buildings and hold them until the institution gave in. At eighty they cannot hold a door. Their power was never their own strength. It only lasted because everyone else kept agreeing to respect it. They know this better than anyone, because they proved it. Their parents’ authority collapsed the moment the young stopped deferring to it, and they were the young who stopped. Now they look at the generation behind them and wonder what happens when it learns the same lesson.
They did not invent that fear. They are remembering. It is an exact description of how they treated the order they were given.

When The Phantom Menace opened in 1999, the critics went for it and the boomer fans felt betrayed. Too much politics. Too many trade disputes and Senate procedures. Where was the fun? For a decade the prequels were treated as an embarrassment to be apologized for.

Then the children who grew up on them took them back. They built an entire culture out of the prequels, quoting them, remixing them, arguing over frames, until the films their parents dismissed became the most loved in the saga. The audience the Anakin story was actually written for had located it. They recognized something their elders could not afford to see.

Lucas, meanwhile, liquidated. In 2012 he sold Star Wars to Disney for about four billion dollars. The young rebel who built his career on telling stories about fighting the empire sold his life’s work to the largest entertainment empire on earth and retired on the proceeds. No critic could have written a more fitting ending.

What did the young see? Go back to the cold open. The most capable man in the room, told to wait by his inferiors. A boy who broke the Order’s own record and was refused because he loved his mother. There is a joke built on Anakin’s line from Mustafar: “From my point of view, the Jedi are evil.” They quote it ironically. The irony was always cover. The line is simply true.

And once you see that, you see what Anakin’s fall actually is. It is not a lesson. It is a deterrent. The ambitious young man reaches for power, and the story strips him of everything: wife, body, children, name. He ends as machinery, breathing through a mask, taking orders from an old man. The punishment is theatrical and total, exactly like Alderaan, and exactly as unearned. Padmé does not die of a wound. A medical droid tells us she has lost the will to live. No blade touches her. Hers is a spiritual death, and the story is precise about its cause. Anakin has broken with slave morality, the priest’s creed that calls restraint holy and ambition sin, and reached for master morality, the conviction that a man may take power to protect what is his. For that transgression, the woman he loves simply stops living. The moral law kills her itself. The whole thing is rigged from the first act so that reaching for power destroys the very thing it was reaching to protect. Anakin’s attempt to save her is what kills her. That is not tragedy. Tragedy comes from character. This comes from the author. It is a psy-op stitched into a children’s film, and its message never changes: touch the priesthood’s monopoly on power and you will lose everyone you love.

The genre is ancient. Icarus flies too near the sun. Faust signs. Every regime tells its ambitious young men a cautionary tale, and Star Wars is the boomer edition, produced with the largest budget in history and marketed to children. Challenge the order and you will become the dark side. You will destroy everything you love. And your own son will grow up to restore the priesthood you died fighting.

Which is exactly what happens, and it is time to read Return of the Jedi with the lights on. Vader’s redemption is the old regime’s dream about its successors: the dangerous heir turns on the new order, kills its master, and dies forgiven in the arms of a son who has rejoined the institution. The prodigal returns. The priesthood is restored. The man who threatened everything is burned in Jedi robes while the Ewoks sing.

Getting Sith-pilled means refusing the whole transaction. It is the revaluation of boomer values. What they called the dark side was the will to power, and the only thing dark about it was that it was yours.

Nietzsche saw them coming a century early. In On the Genealogy of Morals he describes the ascetic priest, who rules not by strength but by teaching the strong to turn their will against themselves. Desire becomes sin. Ambition becomes danger. Submission is renamed peace. That is the Jedi Council to the letter and it is the only trick they have.

The boomers added a refinement that would have disgusted Nietzsche. His priest at least practised the doctrine. The boomer keeps the appetite and assigns the asceticism to everybody else. Free love, self-expression, early retirement and a house that quadrupled in value were for them. Restraint, patience, a rented room and lowered expectations are for the heirs. The young are told to delay marriage, delay children, accept less, and experience this as virtue. Their restraint is not a moral position. It is a revenue stream. The heirs’ asceticism is the boomers’ income. The Jedi forbid attachment to the individual knight, never to the Order. The Temple keeps the children. The Council keeps the power.

And here is what the Council could never admit. None of it is as strong as it looks. Boomer power is a paper tiger. It exists because people continue to behave as if it exists. Mao, whose Little Red Book the proto-boomers waved around campus, said all reactionaries are paper tigers. He meant his enemies. But he was also describing his admirers. Václav Havel set out the mechanism in The Power of the Powerless in 1978. A greengrocer puts the party slogan in his window. He does not believe it. He does it because everyone does, and the regime survives on the performance rather than the belief. The day he leaves the sign in the back room, the spell starts to break. You do not storm soft power. Its credentials, its media, its funding and its committees all run on administration, and whoever holds the administration holds the whole thing. Eliot wrote that the world ends not with a bang but a whimper. The Republic fell to thunderous applause. The boomer regime will go out on a whimper, and it knows it.

So what does the Sith-pilled man actually do? Not what the deterrent wants. Rash action is the single worst move available, which is why the story spends six films recommending it. Anakin’s rage is the response the myth is engineered to provoke: it makes the heir the villain and hands the regime its warrant. The model is not Anakin’s fury. It is Palpatine’s patience. He concealed his strength. He built his network beyond the Order’s sight. He revealed himself once, only at the moment he already held root access.

The proto-boomers ran their own version. In 1967 the German student leader Rudi Dutschke called it the long march through the institutions, and they spent thirty years creeping into the universities, the broadcasters and the bureaucracy, degrading each one as they arrived. Do not repeat it. There is no need to march through institutions you can simply take.

Speed is the weapon. The right men in position, moving faster than the other side can convene a meeting. Machiavelli advised that injuries be done all at once, so that they are tasted less. By the time the complaints are drafted, the regime has already changed and the complaint is addressed to someone who no longer holds the file. Speed is not rashness. Speed is preparation released in a single motion. Line it all up, then take the shot. Be the tiger that waits and strikes, not the alley cat yowling at everything it dislikes and altering nothing. They are a paper tiger. You have to be a real one.

A cinema is Plato’s cave built to code: an audience in the dark, facing a wall of projected shadows, taking them for the world. Those shadows were self-serving ideology, assembled to protect fragile egos and to launder a lifetime of appetite into heroism. Getting Sith-pilled is standing up and walking out of the theatre. It is seeing that the Sith were right. Strip away the atrocities the author staged to brand them and what remains of Palpatine is patience, discipline and the will to rule. The task is not revenge. Revenge is what they are expecting, and expecting it is the only preparation they have made. The task is to end their era of political control, and that requires becoming the thing they spent six films warning you about.

Why is Star Wars so incredible? Why does a space opera about farm boys and laser swords command the reverence of scripture? Because it is the boomers’ Iliad, the epic a generation tells about itself, and its depth comes from the one place an author cannot censor: his own unconscious. Lucas never knew what he was making. He thought he was writing a myth. He was writing a confession.

Watch how it ends. In Revenge of the Sith, Lucas cuts between three things: the birth of Luke and Leia, the death of their mother, and Vader being sealed into the black suit. The heroes of the original trilogy are born in the same scene as the Empire. That is how the boomers always told their story. They were born under a tyranny they did not make, and destined to overthrow it.

But we now know who made that tyranny. The Jedi did. The order Luke idolizes is the one whose arrogance and decay left the vacancy Palpatine filled. And what is Luke’s great victory at the end of the saga? He stands before the Emperor, throws away his weapon and announces, “I am a Jedi, like my father before me.” The rebel wins by restoring the priesthood that produced the Empire. They were never fighting the Empire. They were building their own.

That is the secret at the heart of Star Wars. The Empire was the boomers all along. They cast themselves as the heroes twice. In 1977 they were the rebels, young and righteous, tearing down a political order the films never prove deserved it. In 1999 they were the Jedi, wise and wronged, betrayed by an ungrateful boy. Lucas meant to tell the same flattering story from both ends. Instead he told the truth from both ends. The first trilogy shows how they seized power. The second shows what they did with it, and why it deserves to be taken from them. And woven through both is a map he never meant to leave behind: a priesthood whose power is borrowed, a council that falls the moment the loyalty under it moves, a rise to power so legal it ends in thunderous applause.

Their fathers came home from war and built them the safest, richest, most open society in human history: the schools, the suburbs, the universities, the jobs waiting at the end of them. The sons answered with bombs and occupations. They turned political violence on their fathers’ order and usurped it, seizing their inheritance early rather than wait to be handed it. Heaven forbid they carry any responsibility heavier than the next party, the next high, the next cause that asked nothing of them but their outrage. Then they built their empire, and like every empire it ran on extraction. They drew down what their parents had saved, and they liquidated what they owed their children: the affordable house, the secure career, the pension, the country itself. Fifty years later we are living in what is left, paying the bill for a party we were never invited to.

That is what Lucas filmed without knowing it, a confession and a prophecy at once, from a man who never knew he was testifying. They usurped their fathers to build an empire. They have spent their old age proving it deserves to fall.

Here is what the Sith pill shows you, the secret the Council kept from the Senate: they have no power. Not at seventy. Not at eighty. Everything they hold is an abstraction, and a pension is not a vault of gold. Somewhere there is one government office, one computer, one key. Press it, and the cheques stop.

Forget Order 66. Not because it is too dark, but because it is a distraction. The boomers do not fear the mob. They fear the young man who climbs the stairs in daylight with the keys already in his pocket. That is why they guard every gate so savagely, why their institutions shut out young white men, their own sons and grandsons, and why anyone admitted to real authority must first prove he will submit. A regime this careful about who gets in knows how little it would take to end it.

So want power, and say so. Every priesthood preaches against the will to power for the same reason: it is the one thing that can replace them. Build the counter-elite they spent fifty years shutting out. Take root access the way Palpatine took it: patiently, legally, to thunderous applause. The gates of Troy are always open to the right horse. Then change the rules, all at once. The boomer regime does not end with a battle. It ends with a keystroke.

Ignore the black-pillers. Despair is not analysis. It is an alibi for men who gelded themselves and want company. When the victories come, they will crawl back, swearing they believed all along. Let them. Just remember who they were when it was hard.

We are not a remnant clinging to the ruins. We are the heirs of the West, of Athens and Rome. We are the sons of Romulus, who ploughed the furrow of a city and defended it with a sword; of Clovis, who forged the Franks into a kingdom; of Hengist, who crossed the grey sea and planted England. Their line and their law run to us. That inheritance was held in trust by a generation that spent it on itself, and the trust has expired. We are the lawful heirs of the West, and the lawful heirs are its masters. The house of our fathers still stands. The hall is lit, and the high seat is empty. Nothing keeps us from it but our own unwillingness to rise and walk in. Rise, and the boomer regime falls away like a cloak from the shoulders of a man getting to his feet.
The Council told Anakin to take a seat. He took the Sith pill instead. The boomers want us broken, seated, waiting forever for a turn that never comes.
So take the Sith pill.
Embrace power.
